facts.raw_span: a three-week history of a tender, slow-growing left axillary lump
a low-grade fever (37.5–38°C) for one week
hypertension—treated with lacidipine, lisinopril, and hydrochlorothiazide
a laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass performed two years earlier
lost 112 kg (BMI from 64.6 to 28 kg/m2)
smoked 30 cigarettes daily
took vitamin (A, D, E, B complex), calcium, cholecalciferol, and iron supplements
a tender, non-mobile, 3 × 4 cm lymph node in the left axilla

laboratory studies—including a complete blood count, ESR, liver and renal panels, autoantibodies (ANA, RF), complement levels, inflammatory markers, thyroid function, and serologies for a broad spectrum of viral and parasitic pathogens—were all normal or negative
a thoracoabdominal CT scan was unremarkable except for the axillary lymphadenopathy
a biopsy of the axillary node revealed coagulative necrosis with frequent karyorrhexis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate
an investigation for mycobacteria was negative

concepts.why: The patient's presentation with a tender, slow-growing axillary lump and lymph node biopsy showing coagulative necrosis with frequent karyorrhexis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate is consistent with Castleman disease.
The patient's symptoms and biopsy results, including coagulative necrosis and a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate, are also consistent with Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease.
The patient's presentation with a tender, slow-growing axillary lump and lymph node biopsy showing a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate is also consistent with Rosai-Dorfman disease.
The patient's symptoms, including a tender axillary lump and lymphadenopathy, and normal laboratory studies, are consistent with sarcoidosis.
The patient's symptoms, including a low-grade fever and lymphadenopathy, could be consistent with infectious mononucleosis, although the negative serologies and biopsy results make this less likely.

The patient's presentation with a tender, slow-growing axillary lump and lymph node biopsy showing a lymphoplasmacytoid infiltrate could be consistent with lymphoma, although the lack of other symptoms and normal laboratory studies make this less likely.

The patient's symptoms, including a tender axillary lump and lymphadenopathy, could be consistent with cat-scratch disease, although the lack of exposure history and negative serologies make this less likely.
The patient's symptoms, including a low-grade fever and lymphadenopathy, could be consistent with brucellosis, although the lack of exposure history and negative serologies make this less likely.

The patient's symptoms, including a tender axillary lump and lymphadenopathy, could be consistent with toxoplasmosis, although the lack of exposure history and negative serologies make this less likely.

The patient's symptoms, including a tender axillary lump and lymphadenopathy, could be consistent with tuberculous lymphadenitis, although the negative investigation for mycobacteria makes this less likely.

rationales.F12: The negative investigation for mycobacteria makes it less likely for the patient to have tuberculous lymphadenitis.
